passage: Tushar, you asked me how to help a friend who is quiet. Listen. When I was eleven, my friend Omkar came to school and didn't take out his tiffin. He sat, looking at his hands. I asked, “Are you okay?” He said, “Mm. Fine.” But I stayed near him and didn't push. At the end of the day he said quietly, “My dog is sick.” I said, “I'm sorry.” That was all. If he'd not told me, that would have been all right too. The asking mattered, and the waiting. A friend needs to know you noticed, even if the answer isn't ready yet.

qa.q: How old was the storyteller when Omkar didn't take out his tiffin?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: Why did the storyteller stay near Omkar after he said he was fine?
qa.a: The storyteller sensed something was wrong and wanted him to know someone cared, without pressing him to answer.

qa.q: What can a child do after asking are you okay and hearing fine?
qa.a: Stay nearby, wait and be ready to listen, as the storyteller did.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt when he was asked and then left space?
qa.a: He probably felt cared for and safe enough to share about his dog in his own time.

grounding: A child asks a friend are you okay when noticing quiet behaviour, and the friend may not answer yet.

passage: The lift was stuck and the lights flickered while Gurleen and Nilesh stood inside with two grown-ups. Nilesh was always chatty, but now he was staring at the floor and biting his lip. Gurleen leaned in and whispered, “Are you okay?” Nilesh shook his head slightly. “I don't like small places.” “Want to hold my sleeve?” she said. He took it. She talked softly about her rabbit until the lift jolted and the doors opened. Outside, Nilesh took a big breath. “Thanks for asking,” he said. Gurleen shrugged. “You looked scared.”

qa.q: What did Gurleen talk softly about?
qa.a: Her rabbit.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling in the stuck lift, and what showed it?
qa.a: He was scared of the small space, which showed in his silence, staring at the floor and biting his lip.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that helped in the stuck lift?
qa.a: She asked if he was okay, offered her sleeve and talked calmly about her rabbit.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt when Nilesh thanked her?
qa.a: She may have felt pleased that her question helped, though she shrugged as if it was a small thing. 🙂

grounding: A child asks are you okay when noticing a friend's quiet fear, and the friend answers in the moment.

passage: In the school van crawling through Kolkata traffic, Abhinav sat by the window, not joining the usual fight about songs. He didn't laugh when the driver honked at a cow. Kalyani, beside him, nudged his arm. “Are you okay? You're so quiet.” He shrugged. “Fine. Don't want to talk.” Kalyani nodded and didn't push. She pulled out her chocolate bar and put a piece on his knee. They rode in silence. When the van stopped at his lane, he said, without looking at her, “My dog's sick. The vet's coming today.” Kalyani squeezed his hand. “Tell me tomorrow how he is.”

qa.q: What did Kalyani put on Abhinav's knee?
qa.a: She put a piece of her chocolate bar on his knee.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling as he sat quietly by the window?
qa.a: Abhinav was worried and sad about his sick dog, and not ready to talk about it yet.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do that made it easier for Abhinav to share?
qa.a: She asked kindly, then accepted his no, stayed beside him and offered chocolate without pushing.

qa.q: What would change if Kalyani had kept asking?
qa.a: Abhinav might have closed off completely and not shared the news about his dog at all.

grounding: Shows a child asking a quiet friend are you okay, and the friend not wanting to answer at first.

passage: “Hey. Are you okay?” Sangeeta sat on the step beside Lalremsiami, who had stared at her shoes since the bell. “Mm.” “You didn't eat lunch.” “Wasn't hungry.” Sangeeta waited. “You don't have to tell me. I just noticed.” Lalremsiami picked at her shoelace. “Someone said Mizo food smells weird. I don't want to talk about it more.” “Okay. That was a horrible thing to say. Can we just tell Ma'am, together, before the bus? You don't have to explain much.” A long pause. “Okay.” In the staff room, Ma'am listened and said, “Thank you for telling me. That's not okay, and it's not your fault.” Then she went to find the class before the last bell.

qa.q: What had someone said to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Someone said Mizo food smells weird.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as she stared at her shoes?
qa.a: She was hurt and upset by the unkind comment about her food, and didn't want to talk much about it.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta balance asking and not pushing?
qa.a: She asked gently, said Lalremsiami didn't have to tell her, accepted the short answer and offered to go to Ma'am together that same day.

qa.q: How did Ma'am respond when they told her?
qa.a: Ma'am thanked them, said it wasn't okay and wasn't Lalremsiami's fault, and went to speak to the class before the last bell.

grounding: Shows a child kindly asking a quiet friend are you okay, the friend only partly answering, and a trusted adult acting the same day.

passage: I'm Pankaj. Last month, after Dhruv lost the chess final, he sat on the bench outside the hall with his hood up. I went over and asked, “Are you okay?” He snapped, “Obviously not. Go away.” I felt stung. I almost said something mean back. Instead I said, “Okay. I'll be at the canteen,” and walked off. I kept thinking I'd done it wrong. The next morning Dhruv came and sat next to me at assembly. “Sorry about yesterday,” he said. “I just needed to not talk.” Then he told me about the move he'd missed. Now I know asking is still right, even when the answer is no.

qa.q: What did Dhruv lose?
qa.a: Dhruv lost the chess final.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when Dhruv snapped?
qa.a: Pankaj felt stung and hurt, and briefly wanted to say something mean back.

qa.q: Why was Pankaj's reply after the snap a good choice?
qa.a: Saying where to find Pankaj and then leaving gave Dhruv space while keeping the door open.

qa.q: What did Dhruv need right after the final?
qa.a: Dhruv was upset about losing and needed time not to talk before he was ready to share.

grounding: Shows a child asking a friend are you okay after a loss, and the friend not wanting to answer yet.

passage:
Class note, Thursday, from Usha (class teacher, 4B)

During art, Meenal sat with her crayons untouched, drawing nothing. Gopika noticed before I did. She leaned over and asked quietly, "Are you okay? You're not drawing." Meenal shook her head and said, "Not now." Gopika didn't push. She just slid her own sharpener over and kept colouring beside her.

At lunch I saw Meenal talking to Gopika, and later Meenal told me herself that her cousin, her closest friend, moved to Pune last week. I thanked Gopika privately for noticing. I've added a check-in with Meenal for tomorrow morning.

qa.q: What did Gopika slide over to Meenal?
qa.a: Her own sharpener.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when she noticed Meenal's untouched crayons?
qa.a: Concerned and caring about her friend; she picked up on the quiet, sad behaviour even before the teacher did.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that was kind?
qa.a: She asked quietly, "Are you okay?", accepted "Not now" without pushing and stayed close, so Meenal could talk when ready.

qa.q: How might Meenal have experienced Gopika's quiet company?
qa.a: It likely made Meenal feel cared for without pressure while she was sad about her cousin, which is why she chose to talk at lunch.

grounding: It is a teacher's note on a child asking a quiet friend are you okay, accepting not now, and the friend opening up later.
